position: Additional Areas for Reform (Cyber Threat Intelligence)
proposal: The Mandate recommends that the intelligence community adopt an obligation-to-share policy, with write-to-release products that provide new technical indicators and targeting information relevant to cyber defense to the public or targeted entities within 48 hours of collection, with agency heads able to withhold for operational or counterintelligence reasons but reporting the number and justification of exceptions to Congress. It also calls for a real-time auditing capability that flags unauthorized access, so sensitive intelligence can be shared within the IC.
remaining: An IC-wide policy that makes release of cyber indicators the default within 48 hours.
A real-time audit and identity-management capability for access to shared intelligence.

status_summary: No IC obligation-to-share policy with a 48-hour release rule, exception reporting to Congress, or real-time access auditing was found. The nearest federal action concerns the Cybersecurity Information Sharing Act of 2015, which governs sharing by private companies with the government: it lapsed on 2025-09-30, was extended in a late-2025 stopgap through 2026-01-30, then through 2026-09-30 in a consolidated appropriations act enacted in early February 2026, and a stopgap funding bill passed by the House on 2026-09-01 moves its expiration to 2026-12-11. The National Cyber Director said on 2026-05-07 that the administration wants long-term reauthorization and is developing faster two-way sharing. These steps are parallel and do not set the Mandate's IC release rule.

timeline.event: The original ten-year term of the Cybersecurity Information Sharing Act of 2015 ended; a temporary extension enacted in late 2025 ran through 2026-01-30.
A law-firm post reported that a consolidated appropriations act enacted in early February 2026 (H.R. 7148) had moved the 2015 law's sunset to 2026-09-30.

National Cyber Director Sean Cairncross said the administration is pushing for long-term reauthorization of the 2015 law and is developing faster, more actionable two-way information sharing with the private sector.
The House approved a stopgap funding bill that moves the law's expiration from 2026-09-30 to 2026-12-11; the report said the President was expected to sign it.
A CRS update lists the law's provisions as expiring 2026-12-11 after enactment of the Continuing Appropriations and Extensions Act, 2027.
